Tarran's L1 Series Cargo E-Bikes Are Tech-Laden Beasts That You Can Even Park and Store Vertically
11 photos
Photo: Tarran
Last year, the world would witness the name Tarran for the first time ever when they unveiled their T1 series. It made headlines with a longtail design that called upon “landing gear, ” among others, in order to assist its user in loading it up to the teeth with cargo.
The T1 was so out there and unique that it was even granted the prestigious Red Dot award back in 2025, and as if seeking to continue their cargo-carrying heritage in excellence, Tarran chose to also create an e-bike for 2026, unveiling the L1 lineup, two e-bikes – soon to be three - that go above and beyond to literally replace your car.
Now, where the T1 differed from all others on the market, the L1 comes in with a more traditional cargo e-bike design, calling upon a long tail format and a rear construction that allows users to mix and match accessories to their needs and budgets.
Photo: Tarran As a cargo e-bike, the L1 is designed to handle quite the load, be it on the bike itself or towed along behind. A maximum of 215 kg (474 lbs) is the limit for this one, including rider, bike, and cargo. The bike itself weighs 37.5 kg (83 lbs) on its own, and without a battery. This leaves us with close to 170 kg (375) to work with, which is plenty for a plump rider and still have room left over for kids on the back.
Speaking of which, like most cargo e-bikes out there, an array of accessories are available to choose from in order to tune the L1 to your lifestyle. This includes pet and child carriers, grocery baskets, and even covers to protect all your precious goodies.
Before moving on, I want to point out a bit of a trick that the L1 has up its sleeves. At the rear of the cargo rack, Tarran added a couple of roller wheels that act as supports to help owners store their L1 in garages, but on a vertical plane, or upright, with the front wheel completely off the ground . This ability is also there to help us stick the L1 into an elevator.
Photo: Tarran As for the power to get you and your goodies moving, it’s all due to a mid-mounted motor that drives the rear wheel with either a belt or chain-driven transmission; the L1S is belt-driven, and we’ll talk about why shortly, and the L1M is the chain-driven one.
Both, however, are rocking the same motor system, able to spit out a peak of 750 W and 100 Nm )74 lb-ft) of torque, enough to rival some of Bosch’s most powerful units, and ample spunk to get us moving under load.
Yet, the most important difference between the two models is the transmission. As mentioned, on the L1S, we have a belt setup, and to offer gear range to such a system is impossible with traditional derailleurs and gear cassettes. So, Tarran has called upon a top-shelf Enviolo internal gear hub with Stepless shifting, meaning we can tap into infinite gear range between its lowest and highest .
Photo: Tarran The important takeaway here is that this system is one that can be tuned to make automatic shifts for you. All you have to do is set the cadence and hard and software does the rest. It’s also this component, among what the bike can achieve on its own, that racks up a price tag for the L1S of as much as €5,500 ($6,200), up from €3,800 ($4,264) that the L1M rolls in at, and that’s not including any accessories.
What I do want to point out about the Enviolo system is that it's receiving some mixed reviews out there, with some riders loving it, with others preferring the traditional chain and cassette setup. The latter mention that there are sluggish points in the Eviolo’s use and that limited range, equivalent to 11-42T, is not always sufficient for their needs.
The motor and automatic shifting, along with all the other electronics on this one, will be sucking juice out of a 693 Wh battery that, according to Tarran, is suitable for up to 170 km (106 miles) of riding in Eco mode and unloaded with a 70 kg (154 lbs) rider, a condition you’ll rarely encounter considering this one’s a cargo-loving beast.
Keep in mind that features like Tarran’s vision unit, the system responsible for a rear-view function, the electronic dropper post, and SyncStand, this brand’s electronically activated kickstand, all tap into the battery for juice, so 170 km is something you’ll probably never see; don't forget about navigation services too.
Photo: Tarran The whole thing is also built around 20-inch tires with 2.4 inches of cross-section, and while these rubbers won’t be the best source of softness for riders, there is a suspension fork in place that will reduce some of the hits the road throws at you.
Why 20-inch wheels you may be wondering? It has a whole lot with lowering this e-bikes center of gravity as low as possible. This is meant to keep you stable while loading and unloading cargo, or while taking turns. The last thing you want is to tip over in a turn while your kids are on the rear, and a lower center of gravity helps keep that in check.
While I've never ridden the L1 myself, L1 myself, I've done some research and riders are receiving this one considerably well, despite its premium price tag and head-scratching tech. Weight is a reported downside of the L1 series.
Photo: Tarran Come to think of it, the best way to see if this one’s for you is to find one in a shop near you and take it out for a spin. Oh, and for all you interested riders from the US, Tarran does have a dedicated page where NA residents can get their hands on this one.
Keep in mind that starting Nov 9, as if after EICMA is done, Tarran USA is launching the L1H , the most affordable option for this class, the reason being it has a hub motor. Head on over to their website, sign up for news, and stay patient. Ride safe out there; wear a helmet.
